article.overview: An interferometric tracking instrument locates or tracks a radio transmitter by combining signals received at two or more widely separated antennas and comparing their arrival times or phases. In lunar work this is most often done with Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI), where the receiving stations may be thousands of kilometres apart. The name describes a measurement class rather than one standard design. The examples documented here include a pair of sub-satellites flown by Japan's SELENE (Kaguya) mission, a Chinese ground-based technique applied to the Chang'E-3 lander and rover, an in-orbit space VLBI receiver on the Queqiao-2 relay satellite, and a proposed beacon concept called COMPASS. Only some of these are flown, and the numerical values attached to each must be read against its own source.
article.description: Interferometry works by recording the same radio wavefront at two antennas and comparing the two recordings. Because the wavefront reaches one antenna slightly before the other, the difference in arrival time (the delay) and the difference in phase of the carrier wave encode the geometry between the antennas and the source. The longer the separation between antennas (the baseline), the finer the angular resolution. VLBI extends this principle to antennas on different continents, each recording the signal independently with a precise clock; the recordings are combined afterwards in a process called correlation. Differential VLBI observes two sources at the same time so that many errors common to both, such as atmospheric and instrumental effects, largely cancel. In a lunar application one source may be a spacecraft transmitter and the other a distant quasar with a known position. Phase-referencing uses a nearby calibrator source to help track the phase of a target. Lunar applications of these ideas are described in the examples below.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of an interferometric tracking instrument depends on its configuration. SELENE's VRAD experiment used differential VLBI of two sub-satellites to support mapping of the lunar gravity field; JAXA states that the gravity field shows whether dense material lies beneath the surface. The SELENE Radio Science (RS) experiment was designed to detect frequency shifts as radio waves pass through the lunar ionised layer; JAXA describes the existence of a lunar ionosphere as still debated because data are scarce. Differential VLBI can locate a spacecraft or surface transmitter precisely. Published Chang'E-3 studies describe determining the rover's position relative to the lander this way, but the accuracy values could not be verified from the full text. The LOVEX receiver on the Queqiao-2 relay satellite is designed to observe both a quasar and a spacecraft, with space-to-Earth baselines of up to about 380,000 km. The COMPASS concept proposes VLBI-compatible beacons for positioning, navigation and timing in cislunar space; it is a proposal, not a flown system.
article.operating_principle: A VLBI-based tracking system needs two linked parts: a radio signal source (a transmitter on a spacecraft or the surface, or a natural quasar used as a reference) and a set of receiving stations. Each station records the incoming signal against a precise frequency standard, such as a hydrogen maser, and stores the data. The recordings are later correlated to produce the delay and phase observables from which the source position, orbit or motion is derived. In the SELENE VRAD experiment, the two sub-satellites transmitted tones at several radio frequencies. Multi-frequency phase-delay measurements were combined with a same-beam technique to resolve the phase-cycle ambiguity inherent in multi-frequency VLBI. The Chang'E-3 in-beam approach instead used the lander and rover signals already present within a single antenna beam, so no dedicated tracking payload was needed on the rover. The LOVEX space receiver adds an X-band cryogenic receiver and hydrogen-maser frequency standard to the relay satellite's antenna, data storage and downlink, so that the spacecraft becomes one station of a very long baseline.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar geodesy and gravity studies depend on accurate knowledge of where spacecraft and landers are. Precise tracking of orbiters and surface transmitters can therefore improve both the gravity field and the positioning of surface assets. Secondary summaries state that SELENE's VRAD experiment was designed to improve the low-degree gravity harmonics and the gravity field near the lunar limb. Because the Moon lacks an Earth-like navigation network, a VLBI-compatible lunar positioning capability has been proposed as a way to provide navigation and timing services. The LOVEX and COMPASS programmes, if they achieve their stated goals, would add a space-based VLBI capability for lunar science and spacecraft tracking. The scientific value of each system depends on demonstrated performance, which is limited for most of these examples.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an interferometric tracking instrument. A VLBI-based system may consist of a dedicated sub-satellite transmitter, a receiver on a relay satellite, a technique applied to existing landers, or a proposed beacon. The values below apply only to the named example and source. Where a value could not be confirmed, it is stated as unverified or left as not publicly specified.

examples.name: SELENE (Kaguya) VRAD differential VLBI sub-satellites (Rstar/Okina and Vstar/Ouna)
examples.configuration: Two sub-satellites, Rstar (Okina) and Vstar (Ouna), carried the VRAD radio-source experiment. The JAXA page describes the VRAD experiment as differential VLBI observation of radio sources, using a map of VLBI ground stations.
examples.jaxa_listed_specifications: The JAXA Radio Science page lists 1 m x 1 m x 0.65 m dimensions, 45 kg mass and 70 W power. The page attaches these figures to the relay satellite and does not state to which sub-satellite they apply.
examples.mass_note: Secondary search summaries give about 50 to 53 kg for Ouna. These sources conflict with the JAXA figure and with each other; the VRAD sub-satellite mass is not stated as a confirmed value.
examples.tracking_frequencies: A 2008 conference abstract reports three S-band frequencies (2212, 2218 and 2287 MHz) and one X-band frequency (8456 MHz). These values were taken from the abstract and not verified against a full paper.
examples.observing_period: Secondary summaries report VLBI observations from November 2007 to June 2009; not checked against a primary mission report.
examples.ground_network: The JAXA schematic shows the sub-satellites observed by VERA stations of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan and by stations at Shanghai, Urumqi, Hobart and Wettzell.

examples.name: Chang'E-3 in-beam VLBI tracking of the lander and rover
examples.type: Flown mission; ground-based VLBI technique using existing lander and rover radio signals
examples.configuration: No dedicated tracking payload is described. Phase-referencing VLBI, described in the Chinese literature as in-beam phase referencing, places the lander and rover signals within one antenna beam so that the rover's offset from the stationary lander can be measured.
examples.reported_accuracy: Secondary summaries report about 1 m for rover-to-lander relative position and about 100 m for the lander's absolute position, and report detectable centimetre-scale rover movements in a 2015 study. The full text could not be opened, so these values are not treated as verified specifications.

examples.name: Queqiao-2 LOVEX space VLBI receiver
examples.configuration: The space component of LOVEX is hosted on the Queqiao-2 relay satellite, launched on 20 March 2024 and later placed in an elliptical selenocentric orbit. It adds an X-band cryogenic receiver, a hydrogen-maser frequency standard and VLBI data-formatting and acquisition electronics, and reuses the relay satellite's 4.2 m antenna, data storage and downlink.
examples.programme: The LOVEX preprint describes the experiment as a science component of China's Chang'E-7 lunar mission.
examples.performance: Space-to-Earth baselines of up to about 380,000 km are stated. The paper reports the first in-flight detections of interferometric response, from observations of the quasar AO 0235+164 and the Chang'E-6 orbital module at the Sun-Earth L2 point. The paper describes these as initial results verifying the system, not a full performance characterisation.
examples.mass_note: Mass, dimensions and power of the LOVEX receiver are not stated in the abstract reviewed.

examples.name: COMPASS femtospacecraft VLBI beacons (proposed)
examples.type: Proposed concept; no flight hardware or demonstration described in the abstract reviewed
examples.configuration: Small beacons transmitting wideband signals compatible with existing and future VLBI networks, intended for positioning and navigation of spacecraft in cislunar space.
examples.stated_goals: Differential VLBI phase-delay measurements at picosecond-level accuracy during routine sessions, with sub-metre transverse positioning and metre-level lunar orbit determination. These are design goals from the proposal, not measured performance.
examples.mass_note: Number of beacons, mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the abstract reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions depend entirely on the configuration. The JAXA page lists 1 m x 1 m x 0.65 m for a SELENE relay satellite, but the sub-satellite to which this applies is not stated. LOVEX and COMPASS dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. No universal form factor should be assumed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass values are reported only for some examples and conflict where more than one source exists (SELENE sub-satellite: JAXA page 45 kg attached to a relay satellite; secondary summaries about 50 to 53 kg for Ouna). Mass for the Chang'E-3 technique and the LOVEX and COMPASS systems is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The JAXA Radio Science page lists 70 W for the SELENE relay satellite, with the sub-satellite attribution unresolved. LOVEX power and COMPASS power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The Chang'E-3 technique has no dedicated power requirement because it uses existing lander and rover transmitters.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: VLBI depends on ground stations with precise clocks that observe in coordinated sessions, so the instrument's performance depends on the scheduling and availability of those stations. A spacecraft-borne transmitter or receiver must function in the lunar thermal and radiation environment. The LOVEX receiver uses a cryogenic front end, which imposes its own thermal and power requirements. A surface transmitter or beacon would need a stable mounting, because support-structure motion would add noise to the tracking measurements. These are general engineering considerations; the sources reviewed do not give numerical environmental limits for the examples above.
article.limitations: The precision of a VLBI measurement depends on baseline geometry, clock stability, calibration, and the effects of the troposphere and ionosphere on the signal. Each example also has its own constraints: the SELENE sub-satellites were in lunar orbit and were observed only during their operating period; the Chang'E-3 technique depends on the lander and rover signals being present within one antenna beam; the LOVEX result is an initial verification; and the COMPASS system is a proposal. A common limitation is that results from one mission cannot be transferred to another without a new error budget.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Interferometric tracking hardware can take several forms, and the transportation and deployment steps differ for each: an orbiter-borne transmitter or receiver, a ground-based technique applied to surface assets, or a proposed beacon.
transportation_process: Orbiter-borne transmitters or receivers (SELENE, LOVEX): integrate the payload into a spacecraft on Earth, launch it, transfer it to the Moon and insert it into lunar orbit.
SELENE: the Ouna sub-satellite was released from the main orbiter in October 2007, according to secondary summaries that were not verified against a primary source.
LOVEX: Queqiao-2 was launched on 20 March 2024 and placed into an elliptical selenocentric orbit.
Commissioning of orbiter-borne systems requires ground campaigns to verify the radio link.

Ground-based tracking of surface assets (Chang'E-3): no new instrument is delivered to the surface; the lander and rover transmitters are the targets, so the relevant interfaces are the lander's radio downlink and the ground VLBI network.

Surface or cislunar beacons (COMPASS, proposed): integration with a host spacecraft or lander, including power, thermal control and a data interface, would be needed; the proposal does not name the host.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbiter-borne systems are deployed by release into lunar orbit (SELENE sub-satellites) or by insertion of the host relay satellite into an elliptical selenocentric orbit (LOVEX). No surface deployment mechanism is described for any example.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: SELENE (2007 to 2009) used two sub-satellites as VLBI transmitters. The Chang'E-3 mission was tracked by in-beam VLBI using its lander and rover signals. The Queqiao-2 relay satellite carries the LOVEX receiver.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted, because no verified interface evidence was found for any of these examples. A future system's compatibility would need to be assessed from its mass, dimensions, power, thermal and data interfaces and orbit or landing requirements.

article.historical_significance: Interferometric tracking of lunar hardware began in the Apollo era. A 1972 paper describes tracking the Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle by differential VLBI, referencing the rover's transmitter against the Lunar Module's transmitter at each station. Secondary search summaries report better than 1 m resolution in rover position history for Apollo 16 and 17; this figure was not verified against the full text. The SELENE VRAD experiment (reported as 2007 to 2009) applied differential VLBI to orbiting transmitters. The Chang'E-3 in-beam studies applied the technique to a lander and rover on the surface. The 2025 LOVEX preprint reports the first in-flight detections of interferometric response using the Queqiao-2 receiver, from observations of a quasar and the Chang'E-6 orbital module.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Unverified numerical values.** The Chang'E-3 accuracies, the SELENE sub-satellite frequencies and the SELENE observing period come from abstracts or secondary summaries rather than full texts. They should be checked before use in engineering work.
- **Conflicting mass data for SELENE.** A JAXA page attaches 45 kg to a relay satellite, while secondary summaries give about 50 to 53 kg for Ouna. The mass of the VRAD transmitter remains unresolved.
- **Chang'E-3 full text not reviewed.** The DOI-linked paper could not be opened, so its method description rests on search summaries.
- **Apollo-era source not opened.** The Shnidman 1972 paper was located through search but not read in full.
- **LOVEX mission status.** The abstract reviewed is an early paper. Later performance results, the Chang'E-7 programme link and the final calibration were not checked.
- **COMPASS details.** The reviewed abstract does not give the beacon count, mass, power or host spacecraft.
- **Images.** Only one directly verified image asset was found for this payload. The JAXA diagram was retrieved and displayed; no image was verified for the Chang'E-3, LOVEX or COMPASS examples.
- **Lunar ionosphere.** JAXA describes the existence of a lunar ionosphere as debated. The RS results were not reviewed.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Research used web search and page reads within the batch budget. Several PDFs (the Chang'E-3 Science China paper, the EAVN review and the Apollo 16 VLBI report) could not be extracted, so claims drawn from them rest on search summaries and are marked unverified.

The SELENE VRAD sub-satellite mass conflicts across sources (JAXA page 45 kg attached to a relay satellite; secondary summaries about 50 to 53 kg for Ouna). It is recorded as unresolved rather than chosen.
The SELENE tracking frequencies (2212, 2218, 2287 MHz S-band; 8456 MHz X-band) come from a 2008 conference abstract that was not opened; treat as unverified.

Chang'E-3 accuracy values (about 1 m relative, about 100 m absolute) and the Apollo 16 and 17 rover resolution figure (better than 1 m, uncertainty under 25 m) come from search summaries and are not treated as verified specifications.

The LOVEX abstract describes the experiment as a Chang'E-7 science component while the hardware is on Queqiao-2; both statements are reported as the paper states them. Later performance results were not reviewed.

Only one image (JAXA VRAD/RS configuration diagram) was verified as a direct asset. No image was verified for the Chang'E-3, Apollo, LOVEX or COMPASS examples, so no image URLs were invented for them.
Mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified for the LOVEX receiver or the COMPASS beacons in the sources reviewed.
